extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / practicing chymists and learned readers of natural philosophy (17th-century chemistry audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging claims that substances isolated by chymical operations (especially fire/distillation) are elementary principles; focuses on experimental practice, terminology, and philosophical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and precise terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must not 'play with Names at pleasure' or use equivocal, mystical, or obscure expressions when treating principles; clear and distinct notions are required for speculative enquiries where 'the naked Knowledge of the Truth is the thing Principally aim'd at.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write intelligibly; avoid canting, mystical term usage intended to mystify or to gain admiration. Anti-patterns: deliberate obscurity, ambiguous technical words, mystical secrecy. Good practice: define terms and use them consistently so readers can judge assertions rather than guess intended senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names constrained by descriptive properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author assigns a name (e.g., 'Sulphur') they bind themselves by the properties they ascribe to it (e.g., 'Primogeneal and simple Body, Inflamable, Odorous').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an asserted instance contradicts the described properties (e.g., a body called 'Sulphur' that is uninflamable), one is entitled to disbelieve the naming as mere wordplay. Inventors may coin names, but descriptive claims must be coherent and testable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elemental simplicity must be demonstrated beyond separability by fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances obtained by the action of fire (or other operations) are not therefore necessarily Elements; being separable by fire is insufficient proof of elementary nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require evidence of intrinsic simplicity/purity (not further resolvable) before accepting an isolated substance as elemental. Anticipate further decomposition or resolution into distinct ingredients; do not equate separability with elemental status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not identify elements solely by operational qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The common chymical practice of naming principles from observed operative qualities — 'if they get a Substance inflamable ... they presently call Sulphur; what is sapid and Dissoluble in Water, that must pass for Salt; whatsoever is fix'd and indissoluble in Water, that they name Earth; ... whatsoever Volatile substance they know not what to make of ... they call Mercury' — is unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational qualities (inflammability, solubility, fixedness, volatility) can be produced or altered by texture, treatment, or combination and therefore do not suffice to establish an elemental nature. Require deeper analysis and consistency across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for experimental conditions and apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental setup (open air vs. closed vessels, distillation method, reagents like sal circulatum) materially affects what substances are obtained and their apparent properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating results, report and consider apparatus and conditions; distinguish products of particular methods from putative natural elements. Example: spirits separated by sal circulatum differ from commonly distilled aqua vitae; closed-vessel distillations may yield soot, glass, or mixed products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire can both decompose and recombine — consider secondary formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fire does not always merely resolve or take asunder, but 'may also after a new manner mingle and compound together the parts ... of the Body Dissipated by it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing products of heating/distillation, consider that new compounds (e.g., soot, glass, volatile salts, oils) may form by recombination, inclusion of fiery corpuscles, or association of parts rather than revealing pre-existing simple ingredients. Do not assume products reflect antecedent elemental constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reproducibility and independent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectures or single reported experiments (e.g., Helmont's claims) need reproducible confirmation; one man's relation without means to experiment is weak evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor multiple, repeatable experiments and independent confirmations before accepting extraordinary compositional claims. Treat single, unverified accounts as conjectural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish craft from philosophical account
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'great Difference betwixt the being able to make Experiments, and the being able to give a Philosophical Account of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental procedures (recipes, preparations) should be accompanied by explanatory accounts addressing why outcomes occur. Do not accept mere procedural success as adequate understanding; require interpretation that links operations to hypotheses about nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware assignment of permanence from state-dependent properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities used to name principles (e.g., inflammability, solubility) may change under processes like fermentation, calcination, or distillation so that what appears elemental in one state is altered in another (e.g., spirit of wine transmuted into salt by tartar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether alleged elemental properties persist across different treatments and states; avoid taking transient operational attributes as proof of permanency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test consistency across sources and preparations
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances bearing the same denomination (e.g., 'oyl', 'spirit') obtained from different sources or by different agents (e.g., sal circulatum vs. ordinary distillation) may differ greatly in quality and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that a purported principle displays consistent character regardless of source or method. If properties vary, suspect compound or context-dependent origin rather than elementarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question mystical secrecy and obfuscation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who write darkly and enigmatically about principles or preparations often mask ignorance or invalid doctrine; secrecy is a poor excuse for incomprehensible exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand transparency and intelligibility in descriptions; penalize obscurity that prevents assessment. Anti-patterns: publishing mysteries to impress or conceal; better to omit than to publish unclear accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about inventor's naming rights when claims conflict with observed properties
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'Authors of new Inventions, [have] leave to name them', those names do not exempt claims from critique when descriptions or properties contradict the asserted identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat invented nomenclature as provisional; require that names are substantiated by consistent description and evidence. If the inventor's name obscures contradictions, prefer descriptive terminology tied to observable properties.
